answers.answer: The top region card is revealed and the King is placed there; each player is dealt one region card and places their Grande in that home region. Each player starts with 2 Caballeros in their home region, 1 on scoring-track space 1, and 7 in their court. The summary does not explicitly say how many remain in the provinces, but these are the initial ten asked about.
answers.evidence: Setup: “reveal top card and place the King in that region. Deal one card to each player; they place their Grande in that region (home region).” Each player places “2 Caballeros in their home region, 1 on scoring track space 1, 7 in their court.”

answers.answer: In round 1, the youngest player starts playing power cards; in later rounds, the starting player is whoever played the lowest card last round. The summary does not state the seating direction for the other players. Played values may not match: all values in a round must be different.
answers.evidence: “Starting with the leader (youngest in round 1, then whoever played lowest last round), each player plays one power card face up. All played values must be different.”

answers.answer: Players take turns from highest to lowest power-card value. On their turn, they first add the number of Caballeros shown on their power card from the provinces to their court, then discard that power card, and then select an action card. Thus recruitment precedes action-card selection.
answers.evidence: “Player turns (highest to lowest power card)” and each player “Adds Caballeros from the provinces to their court (number shown on power card)” before “Selects one face-up action card.”

answers.answer: If provinces run out, a player may remove their own Caballeros from the board to their court. The summary says nothing about whether Caballeros in the Castillo may be used this way. The King’s region is expressly protected from movement out, so it cannot supply them. Other protected-location restrictions are unsupported.
answers.evidence: “If provinces run out, a player may remove their own Caballeros from the board to their court.” The King’s Region rule says “No Caballeros, Grandes, or scoreboards may be moved into or out of the King's Region.”

answers.answer: Ordinary deployment may go from the court to regions adjacent to the King’s region or into the Castillo. It may be split among multiple adjacent regions and the Castillo. The printed number is a maximum; the summary does not explicitly say whether using fewer than the full allowance is permitted.
answers.evidence: Deploy from court “to regions adjacent to the King's region or into the Castillo (max shown on card)” and “Can split between multiple adjacent regions and the Castillo.”

answers.answer: Ordinary deployment and the special action may be done in either order, and the special action is optional. Whether the two activities may be interleaved is unsupported.
answers.evidence: The action card’s “two activities (in either order)” are deployment and the special action; the special action is marked “(optional).”

answers.answer: After a player chooses an action card, they turn that card over. The summary does not say what happens to unselected face-up cards at the end of a turn or round. The King card in the 5-Caballero pile is turned face up every round and is never permanently discarded.
answers.evidence: “Turns over the chosen action card.” Also: “The King card (5-pile) is turned face up every round and never permanently discarded.”

answers.answer: Caballeros, Grandes, and scoreboards may not be moved into or out of the King’s region. The summary indicates regions are scored, including the King’s region, and states that its majority holder may receive the King’s bonus when it is scored. Certain action cards can move the King, which changes which region is protected. Other details of that status change are unsupported.
answers.evidence: King’s Region: “No Caballeros, Grandes, or scoreboards may be moved into or out of the King's Region.” “Player with the most Caballeros in the King's Region gets +2 points when it is scored.” Certain action cards “move the King.”

answers.answer: Players announce how many Caballeros they add to the Castillo. The King’s location does not restrict entry: Caballeros can always enter the Castillo. At general scoring the Castillo is scored and then emptied. If the Castillo is scored via an action card, it is not emptied. The summary does not specify any other time when Caballeros may leave.
answers.evidence: “Caballeros placed secretly; players announce how many they add.” They “can always enter the Castillo regardless of King's position.” During general scoring it is “scored, then emptied”; if scored via action cards, “it is NOT emptied.”

answers.answer: General scoring occurs after rounds 3, 6, and 9. In order: each player secretly selects a destination region on their secrecy disk; the Castillo is scored; its Caballeros are moved to their chosen regions; then each region is scored in the order shown on the round chart. Destinations are chosen before the Castillo is revealed/scored.
answers.evidence: “General Scoring (after rounds 3, 6, and 9)” lists: “Each player secretly selects a region,” “Score the Castillo (lift it, count Caballeros…),” “Move Castillo Caballeros to chosen regions,” then “Score each region in order shown on the round chart.”

answers.answer: A given player’s Castillo Caballeros must all go to one region; they cannot choose the King’s region. Keeping them in the Castillo is not listed as an option, and the summary says the Castillo is emptied. The summary does not say what happens if a player selects the King’s region as their destination.
answers.evidence: “Move Castillo Caballeros to chosen regions (all of one player's must go to a single region, cannot be the King's Region).” General scoring says the Castillo is “then emptied.”

answers.answer: The three players tied at four Caballeros each receive the points for the lower tied position, which is third place: 1 point each. The higher tied positions are eliminated. The player with three Caballeros is not assigned points by the summary’s stated tie rule. Grandes do not count as Caballeros in the standard game. The summary does not explicitly state the score for the fourth player in this example.
answers.evidence: For ties: “Tied players each receive the points for the lower position and the higher position is eliminated.” Standard game: a Grande “does not count as a Caballero.”

answers.answer: The player with 4 Caballeros scores first-place value 6, and the player with 3 scores second-place value 4. The players tied at 2 Caballeros occupy the third and fourth positions; the summary’s tie rule awards the lower tied position’s points, but it does not specify the score for fourth place when only three scoring values are listed. Their exact scores are therefore unsupported by the summary.
answers.evidence: Region scoring provides first, second, and third values; ties receive “the points for the lower position and the higher position is eliminated.” The summary does not say what fourth place scores.

answers.answer: The summary lists scoreboards 8/4/0 and 4/0/0 but does not specify which is used in two-player versus three-player games. It also does not state what happens in a two-player tie for first.
answers.evidence: Components lists “2 scoreboards (8/4/0 and 4/0/0),” with no player-count mapping or two-player tie procedure.

answers.answer: When a region is scored, the sole player with the most Caballeros in the King’s region receives a +2 King’s Bonus; it is not awarded on a tied first place. When a region is scored, its sole Caballero-majority holder receives a +2 Home Bonus if their Grande is there; no Home Bonus is awarded for a tied majority.
answers.evidence: King’s Bonus: “+2 points when it is scored” and “Not awarded if tied for first.” Home Bonus: “When a region is scored,” the sole majority holder gains “+2 points if their Grande is in that region”; none “for a tied majority.”

answers.answer: If an action card scores the Castillo, it is not emptied. The summary does not say whether this special scoring redistributes its Caballeros; it only specifies redistribution and emptying during general scoring.
answers.evidence: “If scored via action cards, it is NOT emptied.” General scoring separately says Castillo Caballeros are moved to chosen regions.

answers.answer: The summary says scoreboards may not be moved into or out of the King’s region. It does not say whether a mobile scoreboard can be put at the Castillo, stacked on another scoreboard, or rotated to change values. These requested details are unsupported.
answers.evidence: The only relevant restriction stated is: “No Caballeros, Grandes, or scoreboards may be moved into or out of the King's Region.”

answers.answer: The summary says certain action cards can move a Grande, subject to the King’s Region restriction, and that a Grande marks its owner’s Home Bonus region. It does not give the legal source or destination rules, whether another Grande may already be there, or what changes afterward beyond the Home Bonus location. Those parts are unsupported.
answers.evidence: “Certain action cards can move it, subject to the King's Region restriction.” A Grande “marks the region eligible for its owner’s +2 Home Bonus.”

answers.answer: The summary only says power cards can be recovered via certain action cards. It does not identify which card may be returned, whether the card used this turn can be returned, or whether the choice must be revealed.
answers.evidence: “Power cards are permanently discarded after use (can only be recovered via certain action cards).”

answers.answer: The standard game ends after 9 rounds. The player with the most points wins.
answers.evidence: “After 9 rounds … Player with the most points wins.”
